file=overview.rst
Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px

Just pip install the :code:`rapidfireai` OSS package. It works on a CPU-only machine, a single-GPU machine, 
or a multi-GPU machine. Note that for RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs, GPUs are not needed. 

Launch the server from the command line. Then import it as any other python package in your notebook/script. 
Use our API to define and launch the configs to compare in one go.

file=difference.rst
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

Suppose you have only 1 GPU, say an A100 or H100, and you want to run SFT on a Llama model. 
Current tools force you to run one config after another *sequentially* as shown in the (simplified) illustration below. 
In contrast, by operating on shards, RapidFire AI offers a far more concurrent learning experience by 
automatically *swapping* adapters (and base models, if needed) across GPU(s) and DRAM. 
It does this via efficient shared memory-based caching mechanisms that can spill to disk when needed.

.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px

There are two ways to get started with RapidFire AI for RAG/Context Engineering:

file=overview.rst
Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px

Just pip install the :code:`rapidfireai` OSS package. It works on a CPU-only machine, a single-GPU machine, 
or a multi-GPU machine. Note that for RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs, GPUs are not needed. 

Launch the server from the command line. Then import it as any other python package in your notebook/script. 
Use our API to define and launch the configs to compare in one go.

Postprocess Function
--------------------

Optional user-provided function to postprocess a batch of examples and their respective generated outputs, 
which is injected into this function by the system. 
This is useful for, say, extracting structured information from generations, adding ground truth data, 
or performing any transformations needed before computing metrics.

It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process after generation and before metric computation.
Pass it directly to the :code:`postprocess_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.


.. py:function:: postprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list]) -> dict[str, list]

   :param batch: Dictionary containing a batch of examples, including their respective generated outputs under the reserved key :code:`"generated_text"`.
   :type batch: dict[str, list]

   :return: Dictionary containing the postprocessed batch with any new or modified keys
   :rtype: dict[str, list]


**Examples:**

    # Example 1 from FiQA use case: Adding ground truth documents for retrieval evaluation

        """Function to postprocess outputs produced by generator model"""

API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals
===============

Users can provide the following custom functions as part of their eval config to be used in :func:`run_evals()`.
Note that each leaf config can have its own set of functions for all of these.


Preprocess Function
-------------------

Mandatory user-provided function to prepare the inputs to be given to the generator model. 
It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation.
Pass it directly to the :code:`preprocess_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.

The system injects into this function the batch data, as well as the RAG spec and 
the prompt manager of an individual leaf config.


.. py:function:: preprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list], rag: RFLangChainRagSpec, prompt_manager: RFPromptManager) -> dict[str, list]

   :param batch: Dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values
   :type batch: dict[str, list]

   :param rag: RAG specification object for document chunk retrieval and context serialization
   :type rag: RFLangChainRagSpec

   :param prompt_manager: Prompt manager object for handling instructions and few-shot examples
   :type prompt_manager: RFPromptManager

file=evalsfunctions.rst
def sample_postprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list]) -> dict[str, list]:
		"""Function to postprocess outputs produced by generator model"""

		batch["ground_truth_documents"] = [
			qrels[qrels["query_id"] == query_id]["corpus_id"].tolist()
			for query_id in batch["query_id"]
		]
		batch["answer"] = [extract_solution(answer) for answer in batch["generated_text"]]
		return batch



Eval Compute Metrics Function
-------------------------

Mandatory user-provided function to compute eval metrics on a given batch of (postprocessed) examples, 
which is injected by the system. 
It should return metrics computed over the batch as a whole. 

It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process after generation and postprocessing (if applicable). 
Pass it directly to the :code:`compute_metrics_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.


.. py:function:: eval.compute_metrics_fn(batch: dict[str, list]) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]

Other Eval Config Knobs
------

Finally, apart from the Generator, the following knobs can also be included in your eval config dictionary. Each of 
these can also be a knob set generator, viz., :func:`List()` for a discrete and :func:`Range()` for continuous knobs.

For more details on the four user-given functions listed below, see :doc:`the API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals page</evalsfunctions>`.

For more details on the semantics of the online aggregation strategy arguments listed below, see :doc:`the Online Aggregation for Evals page</onlineagg>`.


**batch_size** : int
	Number of examples to process in one batch for GPU efficiency (if applicable)

**preprocess_fn** : Callable
	User-given function to preprocess a batch of examples; an eval config's RagSpec and PromptManager are input by the system

**postprocess_fn** : Callable, optional
	User-given function to postprocess a batch of examples and generations; a single cfg is passed as input by the system

**compute_metrics_fn** : Callable
	User-given evaluation function to compute eval metrics per batch

file=evalsfunctions.rst
Eval Accumulate Metrics Function
----------------------------

Optional user-provided function to aggregate algebraic eval metrics across all batches of the data. 
If this function is not provided, all metrics returned by :func:`eval.compute_metrics_fn()` 
will be assumed to be distributive (i.e., summed across batches) by default. Use this function 
when metrics require (weighted) averaging or other custom dataset-wide aggregation logic.

It is invoked once at the very end of the evaluation process after all batches have been processed.
Pass it directly to the :code:`accumulate_metrics_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.


.. py:function:: eval.accumulate_metrics_fn(aggregated_metrics: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]

   :param aggregated_metrics: Dictionary with a metric's name as key and a list of per-batch metric dictionaries as values from across all data batches. Inside each value dictionary, at least the reserved key :code:`"value"` will exist that was returned by your :code:`eval_compute_metrics_fn` function.
   :type aggregated_metrics: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]

file=onlineagg.rst
RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach with IC Ops avoids all the above issues,
while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.


Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

file=onlineagg.rst
Of course, batch evals is also *embarrassingly parallel*. So, if you are able to use, say, 
10 machines for the above workload, the two runtimes will come down to 107min vs. 23min.

Note that apart from time, on closed model APIs, your token spend is also reallocated 
to more productive configs, which offers better return on investment for your use case.


Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

file=difference.rst
RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.

The above said, note that downsampling is *complementary* to rapid experimentation--feel free 
do both! The adaptive execution can operate on your downsampled dataset all the same.

file=difference.rst
.. image:: /images/gantt-2gpu.png
   :width: 800px

Likewise, for RAG/context engineering evals on self-hosted LLMs, the above multi-GPU 
scheduling optimizations also apply out of the box, albeit analogous to a single epoch. 
When using only closed model APIs such as OpenAI, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically 
optimizes how CPU cores and the token rate limits are apportioned across configs. 
This will help avoid wastage of token spend on unproductive RAG configs and help you 
redirect the spend to more productive RAG configs in real time.


Why Not Just Downsample Data?
------------

At first glance, one might consider running multi-config comparisons by downsampling data for 
quick estimates, then running promising configs on full data. While common, this approach is 
often misleading and cumbersome.

A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

file=onlineagg.rst
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

This means you get **running metric estimates with confidence intervals** in real time. 
So, you can confidently stop poor configs earlier, clone better configs on the fly, and 
perform more informed exploration to reach much better eval metrics in much less time.

Multi-GPU Model Support
------

Ordinarily, any given run's model(s) for its batch size must fit on a single GPU's memory. 
For DPO and GRPO, both the policy and reference models must fit on the GPU together. 

For SFT (and DPO), RapidFire AI can use FSDP automatically to partition a large model across GPUs on the same machine.
Provide the FSDP usage details in a config knob. See :doc:`the SFT page</sft>` FSDP section for more deatils.

We also plan to add support for multi-GPU model partitioning via DeepSpeed soon.

If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:

* Run the command :code:`ps - ef | grep python`, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command :code:`kill -9 [PID]`.

* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.

* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.


Recovering Storage Space
-------

If you run out of storage space on your machine due to experimenting with lots of LLMs, we 
recommend clearing out the ".cache" folder on your home directory that is created by 
Hugging Face to import the base models. 
One experiment's imported models are not needed for another; so, it is safe to delete them.

If you want to reclaim even more space, look at the artifacts from your experiments and 
either delete some of the files or move them to other/remote storage. 
Note that when you use LoRA adapters, RapidFire AI saves only the trained adapters in the 
checkpoints of the runs, not the base models.

API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.

API: Generator Configs
===============

RapidFire AI supports both self-hosted open LLMs and closed model LLM APIs as the generator. 
As of this writing, it wraps around the model config of vLLM for the former and the OpenAI API for the latter. 
We plan to expand support for more generator plugins, including Gemini and Claude APIs, based on feedback. 


RFvLLMModelConfig
------

This is a wrapper around vLLM's :class:`config` and :class:`SamplingParams` classes. 
The full list of their arguments are available on `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/config/index.html>`__ 
and `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.6.4/dev/sampling_params.html>`__, respectively.

The difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued or 
:class:`Range` valued in an :class:`RFvLLMModelConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can 
be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

This is a wrapper around OpenAI's API client config and chat completion parameters. 
The full list of their arguments are available on `this page <https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat/create>`__.

The difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued or 
:class:`Range` valued in an :class:`RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can 
be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

.. py:class:: RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig

All configs are executed on the first 1/8th of the data (50 examples), with 
their **incrementally computed** eval metrics shown in real time with confidence intervals. 
In the figure, the 3 worst configs are stopped, while the best is cloned to add 2 new variants. 
The 3 running configs now continue on the second 1/8th of the data (cumulatively, 
100 examples), and so on.
One clone is then stopped halfway through the aggregation, while the other two run to completion. 
Ultimately, the other clone ends up being the best config overall.

Note that the confidence intervals shown will keep narrowing as configs see more shards, converging 
to zero when 100% of the data is seen, i.e., the metrics become exact point estimates.
Overall, compared to sequential batch evals in which the original 4 configs all run to completion, 
RapidFire AI enables you to explore more configs in less time, while reaching better eval metrics.

while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in

Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

file=onlineagg.rst
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

This means you get **running metric estimates with confidence intervals** in real time. 
So, you can confidently stop poor configs earlier, clone better configs on the fly, and 
perform more informed exploration to reach much better eval metrics in much less time.

reference_answer: RapidFire AI currently supports two knob set generators: List() for a discrete set of values and Range() for sampling from a continuous value interval. List() takes a list of discrete values where all values must be the same Python data type. Range() takes a start, end, and dtype parameter (either 'int' or 'float') and performs uniform sampling within the given interval.

Traditional tools force you to run one config after another sequentially. In contrast, RapidFire AI's adaptive execution engine shards the dataset randomly into chunks and schedules all runs on one shard at a time, then cycles through all shards. This enables interruptible execution across GPUs/CPUs, providing a far more concurrent learning experience by automatically swapping adapters and base models across GPUs and DRAM via efficient shared memory-based caching mechanisms. The swapping overhead is minimal, less than 5% of runtime. This means before the third model config even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows learning behaviors of all configs on the first 2-3 chunks.

The Experiment constructor accepts three parameters: (1) experiment_name (str), a unique name for the experiment used to collate plots on the dashboard and for saving artifacts; (2) mode (str), either 'fit' or 'eval' with default 'fit'; and (3) experiments_path (str, optional), the path to a folder to store experiment artifacts, defaulting to './rapidfire_experiments'.

RFGridSearch requires each knob to have either a single value or a List() of values, but no knob should have a Range() of values or it will error out. RFRandomSearch allows each knob to have a single value, a List() of values, or a Range() of values. Its sampling semantics are independently-identically-distributed (IID): it uniformly randomly picks a value from each discrete set and from each continuous set to construct one knob combination, then repeats this process to accumulate num_runs distinct combinations.

For RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs (like OpenAI), GPUs are not needed. Install RapidFire AI with 'pip install rapidfireai' (requires Python 3.12+), then run 'rapidfireai init --evals' to initialize for RAG evals, and then 'rapidfireai start' to start the server. Starting the server is optional for run_evals() since results are also shown in an in-notebook table and IC Ops can be displayed in the notebook. Provide a valid OpenAI API key via a config argument as shown in the GSM8K and SciFact tutorial notebooks.

RapidFire AI supports four IC Ops: (1) Stop - earmarks a run to be stopped at the end of its current chunk, keeping it alive but not using GPU resources from the next chunk; (2) Resume - applicable only to previously stopped runs, earmarks them to be resumed from the next chunk onward; (3) Clone-Modify - allows adding clones of a chosen parent run with editable config knobs, optionally warm-starting with the parent's weights; (4) Delete - earmarks a run to be deleted from the next chunk onward, making its curves vanish from the plots, though model checkpoints are preserved in the experiment artifacts.

The preprocess_fn is a mandatory user-provided function that prepares the inputs to be given to the generator model. It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation. The system injects three arguments: (1) batch - a dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values; (2) rag - an RFLangChainRagSpec object for document chunk retrieval and context serialization; (3) prompt_manager - an RFPromptManager object for handling instructions and few-shot examples. The function must return a dictionary with a reserved key 'prompts' containing the fully formatted prompts for the generator.

RapidFire AI supports three vector store backends: (1) FAISS - an in-memory store that is the default and requires no setup, but only supports Create mode since it is not persistent; (2) PGVector (PostgreSQL) - a persistent vector store that supports Create, Read, and Update modes; (3) Pinecone - a cloud-hosted persistent vector store that also supports Create, Read, and Update modes. In Read mode, you retrieve from a pre-existing index. In Update mode, you add new content to an existing index. Using PGVector or Pinecone in Read mode is especially useful for efficient experimentation since you preprocess and embed your corpus once and then run many retrieval/generation configurations against the same index.

The DataFrame returned by get_runs_info() contains the following columns: run_id, status, mlflow_run_id, completed_steps, total_steps, start_chunk_id, num_chunks_visited_curr_epoch, num_epochs_completed, error, source, ended_by, warm_started_from, and config (the full config dictionary).

The three supported search algorithm types are: (1) 'similarity' - standard cosine similarity search, which is the default; (2) 'similarity_score_threshold' - similarity search with a minimum score threshold (SST), which additionally accepts a 'score_threshold' parameter; (3) 'mmr' - Maximum Marginal Relevance search for diversity, which additionally accepts 'fetch_k' (number of documents to fetch before MMR reranking, default 20) and 'lambda_mult' (diversity parameter balancing relevance vs. diversity, default 0.5). All three types support a 'k' parameter for the number of documents to retrieve (default 5) and an optional 'filter' parameter.

Online aggregation is a technique adapted from database systems research that provides running metric estimates with confidence intervals in real time as shards of the evaluation dataset are processed. This enables stopping poor configs earlier and cloning better configs on the fly. RapidFire AI supports three confidence interval strategies: (1) Normal Approximation - the default strategy using the Central Limit Theorem, suitable for non-trivial sample sizes (n > 30); (2) Wilson Score - better for small sample sizes or metrics near 0/1 boundaries, more robust for extreme proportions; (3) Hoeffding Bounds - best for maximum safety with guaranteed coverage, making no distributional assumptions but producing typically loose intervals. All three support optional Finite Population Correction (FPC).

When using the Clone-Modify IC Op, you can warm-start a clone using its parent's weights by enabling the warm-start option. Warm-started clones inherit their parent's learning behavior so far and can reach better eval metrics faster. However, warm starting is only allowed if the clone has identical neural architecture as the parent, including LoRA adapters; otherwise, it will error out. You can edit other knobs such as learning rate in the clone, but the model architecture and LoRA configuration must match the parent's for warm starting to work.

The accumulate_metrics_fn is an optional user-provided function that aggregates algebraic eval metrics across all batches of data. It is invoked once at the very end of the evaluation process after all batches have been processed. If this function is not provided, all metrics returned by the compute_metrics_fn will be assumed to be distributive (i.e., summed across batches) by default. This function is needed when metrics require weighted averaging or other custom dataset-wide aggregation logic. The return dictionary can include optional keys 'is_algebraic', 'is_distributive', and 'value_range' to support online aggregation.

RapidFire AI's current default dashboard is a fork of the popular OSS tool MLflow. It also supports TensorBoard and Trackio for logging metrics. Support for Weights & Biases and CometML is coming soon. You can specify which dashboards to use in two ways: (1) via the server start command with 'rapidfireai start --tracking-backends [mlflow | tensorboard | trackio]'; or (2) via environment variables in your Python code/notebook by setting RF_MLFLOW_ENABLED, RF_TENSORBOARD_ENABLED, and RF_TRACKIO_ENABLED to 'true'. You can use any one, two, or all three dashboards simultaneously.

The key LoRA knobs typically experimented with are: (1) r (rank) - the most critical knob, typically a power of 2 between 8 and 128, where higher rank means higher adapter learning capacity but slightly higher GPU memory footprint; (2) lora_alpha - controls adaptation strength, typical values are 16, 32, and 64, usually set to 2x the rank; (3) target_modules - which layers to apply LoRA to, common options being query/value only ['q_proj', 'v_proj'], query/key/value, or all linear layers; (4) lora_dropout - controls regularization, typically between 0.0 to 0.05. A common starting combination is rank 16 and 32 (with alpha 32 and 64 respectively) targeting only query/value projection modules, then expanding based on observed loss and eval metrics behavior.

When constructing a config group with List() or Range(), if the assigned search k value is less than the assigned reranker top_n value, the combination is meaningless and will be omitted automatically by RapidFire AI. All other combinations create valid runs. For example, if k is List([5, 10]) and top_n is List([5, 6]), then in the 2x2 grid, the combination k=5 and top_n=6 will be automatically omitted but the other 3 combinations will be valid.

RapidFire AI requires Python 3.12+. You should verify that your shell's python3 resolves to Python 3.12 before creating the virtual environment. If you encounter any error, you can run the diagnostic command 'rapidfireai doctor' to get a complete diagnostic report covering the Python environment, relevant packages, GPU/CUDA status, and key environment variables.

The document_template is an optional function that formats each retrieved chunk for context injection into prompts. It accepts a single LangChain Document object and returns a formatted string. Multiple documents are separated by double newlines when serialized. If not provided, the default template formats each document by joining all metadata key-value pairs with semicolons, followed by a newline and the document's page_content. Users can provide custom templates to control what metadata fields are included, for example including only the document source or a title field that was ingested via metadata_func in the document loader.

Unlike run_fit() which returns None, run_evals() returns a dictionary with the run/config ID as the key. The value is a 2-tuple containing two dictionaries: one for all aggregated metrics and one for all cumulative metrics. Within an experiment, you can rerun run_evals() as many times as you want, and all runs will be overlaid on the same plots on the ML metrics dashboard. The function also supports providing various config combinations including single config dictionaries, lists of configs, or config group generator outputs like RFGridSearch() and RFRandomSearch().

RapidFire AI supports two types of generator configs: (1) RFvLLMModelConfig, which wraps around vLLM's config and SamplingParams classes for self-hosted open LLMs; and (2) RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig, which wraps around OpenAI's API client config and chat completion parameters for closed model LLM APIs. Support for additional generator plugins including Gemini and Claude APIs is planned. In both cases, individual arguments (knobs) can be List or Range valued for multi-config specification.

The sampling_params dictionary in RFvLLMModelConfig controls sampling behavior during text generation by vLLM. The recommended knobs include: 'temperature' (a float controlling randomness where lower values are more deterministic and 0.0 means greedy sampling, default 1.0), 'top_p' (a float controlling cumulative probability of top tokens to consider, must be in (0,1], default 1.0), and 'max_tokens' (maximum number of tokens to generate per output sequence). All knobs in this dictionary are passed to vLLM as-is, and vLLM uses its defaults for unspecified knobs.

RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig provides two rate limiting parameters: rpm_limit (requests per minute) and tpm_limit (tokens per minute) to the OpenAI API. These are used for throttling to avoid exceeding OpenAI API quotas. Users should check the rate limits published by OpenAI for details on their tier and the latest per-model limits. When using closed model APIs, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically optimizes how CPU cores and token rate limits are apportioned across configs to avoid wastage of token spend on unproductive RAG configs.

RFPromptManager provides semantic similarity-based example selection to construct prompts with the most relevant examples for each input query. It uses an embedding_cfg to compute semantic similarity between examples and queries, where the embedding class (such as HuggingFaceEmbeddings or OpenAIEmbeddings) is specified as a dictionary with the class itself as value (not an instance). The example_selector_cls parameter determines the selection strategy - either SemanticSimilarityExampleSelector for pure similarity or MaxMarginalRelevanceExampleSelector for diversity. The k parameter controls how many examples to retrieve per query (default 3). Each example is formatted using an example_prompt_template with placeholders matching the keys in the example dictionaries.

Apart from the Generator, the following knobs can be included in the eval config dictionary: batch_size (number of examples per batch), preprocess_fn (mandatory function to preprocess a batch), postprocess_fn (optional function to postprocess a batch after generation), compute_metrics_fn (mandatory function to compute eval metrics per batch), accumulate_metrics_fn (optional function to aggregate algebraic metrics across batches; if not given, all metrics are assumed distributive), and online_strategy_kwargs (optional dictionary for online aggregation with keys 'strategy_name', 'confidence_level' defaulting to 0.95, and 'use_fpc' defaulting to True). Each of these knobs can also be a List() or Range() knob set generator.

The create_model_fn is a mandatory user-provided function that must return a tuple of (model, tokenizer), specifically a HuggingFace PreTrainedModel and PreTrainedTokenizer. It receives a model_config dictionary as input, which is injected by RapidFire AI with all key-value pairs for one model config output by the config-group generator. This function is invoked when a trainer object is created for each run. Inside it, users can use whatever knobs they set in the config group, such as model type or name, to instantiate a model accordingly. Models can be imported from the Hugging Face model hub or loaded from local checkpoint files.

Reward functions are user-provided functions needed for GRPO that evaluate generated outputs during training. TRL injects lists of prompts, completions, completion IDs, and trainer state as keyword arguments. Users can use only a subset of these in their reward function signature as long as they include **kwargs. Depending on the dataset format, prompts and completions will be either lists of strings (standard format) or lists of message dictionaries (conversational format). The return type must be a list of floats (one per completion), or None for examples where the reward function is not applicable. Multiple reward functions can be passed as a list to the reward_funcs argument of RFModelConfig, and multiple variants of these lists can be used as a List for multi-config specification.

RFSFTConfig is a wrapper around HuggingFace TRL's SFTConfig class that preserves all its semantics under the hood. The only difference is that individual arguments (knobs) can be List or Range valued for multi-config specification. Key configurable arguments include learning_rate, lr_scheduler_type, per_device_train_batch_size, per_device_eval_batch_size, gradient_accumulation_steps, num_train_epochs, logging_steps, eval_strategy, eval_steps, fp16/bf16, and save_strategy. For larger LLMs that need cross-GPU model partitioning, you can also specify FSDP configuration using the fsdp and fsdp_config arguments with settings like sharding strategy, auto-wrap policy, and offloading parameters.

Both RFDPOConfig and RFGRPOConfig are wrappers around their corresponding HuggingFace TRL classes (DPOConfig and GRPOConfig respectively). RFDPOConfig includes DPO-specific arguments such as model_adapter_name, ref_adapter_name, force_use_ref_model, loss_type (e.g., 'sigmoid'), beta (controlling divergence from reference model), max_prompt_length, and max_completion_length. RFGRPOConfig includes GRPO-specific arguments such as num_generations (number of generated completions per prompt) and similar training parameters. A key difference is that RFDPOConfig supports FSDP for cross-GPU partitioning, while out-of-the-box FSDP support for GRPO is still in the works as of this writing.

A leaf config is a single combination of knob values in a config dictionary. In a config dictionary, a knob's value can be a singleton or set-valued (using List or Range). When set-valued knobs are fed to a config-group generator method, each unique combination produced is called a leaf config. RapidFire AI instantiates one run per leaf config, and its values are injected via the model_config argument to the user's create_model_fn() function. A run is a central concept representing this single combination of configuration knob values, and RapidFire AI assigns each run a unique integer run_id within an experiment.

The main Experiments page on the dashboard has 4 main tabs: (1) Table - shows a view of an experiment with all its runs where each run represents one model with one set of config knob values; (2) Chart - shows metrics plots with one plot per metric spanning loss on training and evaluation sets as well as all named metrics from the compute_metrics() function; (3) Experiment Log - a continually appending message log displaying all operations run with RapidFire AI's API; (4) Interactive Control (IC) Log - a continually appending log specifically displaying all IC operations done via the IC Ops panels.

If you run out of storage space, RapidFire AI recommends clearing out the '.cache' folder on your home directory, which is created by Hugging Face to import base models. One experiment's imported models are not needed for another, so it is safe to delete them. For additional space, you can look at the artifacts from your experiments and delete or move them to other/remote storage. Notably, when using LoRA adapters, RapidFire AI saves only the trained adapters in the run checkpoints, not the base models, which keeps checkpoint sizes manageable.

The SFT tutorial uses the 'Bitext customer support' dataset for creating a customer support Q&A chatbot. It uses a sample of 5,000 training examples and 200 evaluation examples for tractable demo runtimes. The full version compares 2 base model architectures: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, while the lite version uses only TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0. There are 2 different LoRA adapter configurations: a low-capacity adapter (rank 16; 8 for lite) targeting 2 modules and a high-capacity adapter (rank 128; 32 for lite) targeting 4 modules, totaling 4 combinations launched with grid search.

The DPO tutorial explores 4 configurations using the Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 base model with 4-bit quantization (QLoRA): (1) Basic Bradley-Terry - standard sigmoid loss with medium capacity LoRA (rank 64) and large beta; (2) High divergence - high capacity LoRA (rank 128) with small beta to encourage divergence from the reference model; (3) Robust loss - uses robust loss type with label smoothing to handle noisy preference data; (4) Combined loss - a weighted combination of sigmoid, BCO pair, and SFT losses. The training starts from a pre-trained SFT model (rapidfire-ai-inc/mistral-7b-sft-bnb-4bit) to ensure the model distribution is suitable for DPO alignment training.

The GRPO tutorial uses 5 custom reward functions: (1) Correctness reward - awards 2.0 points for matching the ground truth answer exactly; (2) Integer reward - awards 0.5 points for producing numeric answers, validating output format; (3) Strict format reward - awards 0.5 points for exact XML formatting compliance; (4) Soft format reward - awards 0.5 points for flexible XML formatting with more lenient matching; (5) XML count reward - a fine-grained reward of up to 0.5 points for proper XML tag usage and structure. The whole set of reward functions is used for all configs, and GRPO uses multiple reward functions to provide richer training signals.

The SciFact tutorial uses an all-closed model API workflow (no GPU needed) with the following RAG components: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small for embeddings, FAISS with CPU-based exact search (no ANN approximation) as the vector store, 512-token chunks with 32-token overlap using recursive character splitting with tiktoken encoding, top-15 initial retrieval, cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 reranker with top-5 final documents, and a custom document template including document titles with content. It compares 2 generator models via OpenAI API (gpt-5-mini and gpt-4o) across 2 different retrieval/search strategies (similarity search and MMR), for a total of 4 combinations launched with grid search.

The GSM8K tutorial uses a hybrid workflow with a self-hosted open LLM for embeddings and OpenAI API calls for generation. The few-shot prompting pipeline uses semantic similarity-based example selection with sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, drawn from a pool of 10 hand-crafted examples covering diverse problem types. It uses chain-of-thought style prompt templates with step-by-step reasoning and final answers after '####'. It compares 2 generator models (gpt-5-mini and gpt-4o), with 2 different reasoning effort levels (medium and high) for gpt-5-mini only, and 2 different few-shot k values (3 and 5 examples per prompt). This produces 6 total combinations via a union of two grids: 1x1x2 + 1x2x2 = 6.

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms LLM pipeline customization from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization. It is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between: the IDE where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend. It works on a CPU-only machine, a single-GPU machine, or a multi-GPU machine, and for RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs, GPUs are not needed.

RapidFire AI provides three RAG/context engineering tutorials, each demonstrating a different workflow type: (1) FiQA RAG Q&A chatbot - an all-local model workflow with self-hosted open models from Hugging Face for both embedding and generation; (2) SciFact RAG for scientific claim verification - an all-OpenAI workflow using OpenAI calls for both embedding and generation (no GPU needed); (3) GSM8K few-shot/context engineering for math reasoning - a hybrid workflow spanning a self-hosted open LLM for embeddings and OpenAI API calls for generation.

RapidFire AI’s **adaptive execution engine** turns a multi‑config run into a *shard‑by‑shard, interrupt‑and‑resume* workflow instead of the classic “run one config to completion, then start the next” approach.

Its purpose is to perform any per‑batch transformations needed before metrics are calculated—e.g., extracting structured fields from the generations, adding ground‑truth data, or otherwise reshaping the batch.

**When it runs:**

RapidFire AI says that down‑sampling alone is a static, manual shortcut that misses the core benefits of its **online‑aggregation** engine:

* **You must pick a sample size up‑front** – a hard choice when eval metrics have high variance, and a wrong size can give misleading point estimates.  
* **No confidence intervals** – down‑sampled results are just point estimates, so you can get false confidence in a config.  
* **Manual re‑sampling is required** to reduce variance, which adds tedious file‑juggling and extra compute.  
* **No dynamic experiment control** – you cannot stop a poor config early, clone or modify a promising one on the fly, or resume/abort runs without re‑implementing that logic yourself.  
* **No automated parallelism or IC‑Ops** – down‑sampling does not leverage shard‑based parallel execution, token‑rate scheduling, or GPU/CPU allocation, so token spend and compute are often wasted on unproductive configs.

In contrast, RapidFire AI’s online aggregation shards the data, runs many configs in parallel, and streams **real‑time metric estimates with statistically‑sound confidence intervals**, letting you stop bad configs early, clone good ones, and continuously re‑allocate token/compute resources for maximum efficiency.

In RapidFire AI’s online‑aggregation engine the metric’s **aggregation semantics** determine how the per‑shard results are combined:

| **Metric type** | **What it means** | **What you must provide** |
|-----------------|-------------------|---------------------------|
| **Distributive** | The metric can be computed on each shard (batch) and then combined with a simple, built‑in algebra (e.g., sum, count, average). No extra code is needed – if you don’t supply an `accumulate_metrics_fn`, all metrics returned by `compute_metrics_fn` are treated as distributive. | Nothing extra; the engine aggregates them automatically. |
| **Algebraic** | The metric’s final value cannot be obtained by a naïve sum/average of shard‑level values; it needs a custom reduction (e.g., variance, F1‑score, or any metric that requires both numerator and denominator to be merged in a specific way). | You must supply an `accumulate_metrics_fn` that knows how to combine the algebraic pieces across batches. |

So, **distributive metrics are directly aggregatable by the system, while algebraic metrics require a user‑provided aggregation function to correctly combine the intermediate results.**

RapidFire AI’s **adaptive execution engine** turns a multi‑config run into a *shard‑by‑shard, interrupt‑and‑resume* workflow instead of the classic “run one config to completion, then start the next” approach.

* **Sharding vs. whole‑dataset passes** – The engine first splits the training/evaluation data into random “chunks” (shards). It then runs *all* configs on a single shard, swaps to the next shard, and repeats, so no config ever has to wait to see the entire dataset before another config can start.

* **Interruptible, concurrent execution** – Because each config only holds a shard in memory, RapidFire can pause, stop, resume, clone or modify any run on‑the‑fly. Traditional pipelines are sequential and block until an epoch (or full eval) finishes.

* **Automatic model/adapter swapping** – RapidFire swaps adapters (and even base models) across GPU(s) and DRAM using a shared‑memory cache that can spill to disk when needed. Conventional tools keep a single model loaded for the whole run.

* **GPU utilisation** – Even on a single GPU you can launch many configs (e.g., 8‑14 configs) simultaneously; the scheduler moves work across GPUs/CPUs automatically, avoiding the under‑utilisation common in task‑parallel or data‑parallel sequential runs.

In short, RapidFire’s adaptive engine shards the data, interleaves configs per shard, and provides interruptible, cache‑driven, multi‑GPU scheduling—giving far more concurrent, flexible experimentation than the traditional sequential execution model.

**Online aggregation** in RapidFire AI evals means that the evaluation data set is split into uniformly‑random shards and each config processes the shards one‑by‑one (in parallel with other configs). After each shard the system updates the metric estimates **incrementally** and shows **real‑time confidence intervals** that shrink as more shards are seen, eventually converging to exact point estimates when the whole data set has been processed. This enables early stopping of poor configs, cloning of promising ones, and much faster, lower‑cost experimentation.

`accumulate_metrics_fn` is an optional user‑provided callable that runs **once, after all batches have been processed**, to combine the per‑batch metric dictionaries returned by `eval.compute_metrics_fn` into final dataset‑wide values. It is needed for metrics that are not simply additive—e.g., those that require weighted averaging, custom aggregation, or other algebraic handling.

**If omitted**  
When `accumulate_metrics_fn` is not supplied, the eval system assumes every metric returned by `eval.compute_metrics_fn` is **distributive** and automatically **sums** the per‑batch `"value"` fields to produce the final metric. No custom aggregation is performed.

**`document_template` in `RFLangChainRagSpec`**

- **Purpose** – It is an optional callable that formats each retrieved **LangChain `Document`** before the chunks are injected into the prompt.  
- **Signature** – `def my_template(doc: Document) -> str`.  
- **Behavior** – The function receives a single `Document` and must return a string. When several documents are used, RapidFire AI concatenates the returned strings with **double newlines** (`"\n\n"`).  
- **Customization** – By providing your own function you can decide which metadata fields to include, how they are ordered, and how the page content is presented (e.g., only `source`, custom prefixes, etc.).

**Default template (used when `document_template` is omitted)**  

```python
def default_template(doc: Document) -> str:
    """Default document formatting template."""
    metadata = "; ".join([f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in doc.metadata.items()])
    return f"{metadata}:\n{doc.page_content}"
```

- It **includes all metadata key‑value pairs**, joined by `"; "` and placed on the first line.  
- The document’s `page_content` follows on the next line.  
- This string is then used for each chunk, and multiple chunks are separated by double newlines.  

Thus, `document_template` lets you control context formatting, while the built‑in default simply lists every metadata entry followed by the document text.

`RFPromptManager` builds the few‑shot part of a prompt by **choosing the most semantically similar examples to the current query**.  

1. **Embeddings** – The manager is given an `embedding_cfg` (e.g., a HuggingFace sentence‑transformer). It uses this to embed every example in the pool and the incoming user query.  
2. **Similarity selector** – With `example_selector_cls=SemanticSimilarityExampleSelector`, it computes similarity (typically cosine) between the query embedding and each example embedding.  
3. **Top‑k selection** – It returns the `k` highest‑scoring examples (where `k` can be a single value or a `List` of values, e.g., `[3, 5]`).  

Thus, for each input query `prompt_manager.get_fewshot_examples(user_queries=…)` returns the dynamically chosen few‑shot examples that are most relevant according to semantic similarity.

| **batch_size** | `int` | Number of examples processed per batch (used for GPU efficiency when applicable). |

| **postprocess_fn** | `Callable` (optional) | User‑provided function that post‑processes a batch of examples and the generated outputs; the system passes a single config as input. |
| **compute_metrics_fn** | `Callable` | User‑provided evaluation function that computes the desired metrics for each batch. |

These knobs can be specified directly (as singletons) or as set‑valued knobs using `List()` or `Range()` generators, just like other config parameters.

In GRPO you supply one or more **user‑defined reward functions** and list them in the `reward_funcs` field of an `RFModelConfig`.  
During training the underlying Hugging Face TRL trainer calls each function **on‑the‑fly** for every generated output, passing the data it already has.

**Signature that TRL injects**

```python
def reward_function(
    prompts,            # List[str] or List[List[Dict[str,str]]]
    completions,       # List[str] or List[List[Dict[str,str]]]
    completions_ids,   # List[List[int]]  (token IDs of the completions)
    trainer_state,     # current TrainerState object
    **kwargs           # any additional keyword args TRL may add
) -> List[float]:      # one reward per completion
```

So the trainer supplies the original prompts, the generated completions (both raw text and token IDs), the current `trainer_state`, and any extra keyword arguments. Your function returns a list of float rewards—one per completion—that GRPO then uses as its multi‑reward signal.

**RFSFTConfig** is essentially a thin wrapper around Hugging Face TRL’s **`SFTConfig`**.  
All training‑specific knobs that you would normally pass to `SFTConfig` (learning‑rate, batch size, number of epochs, optimizer settings, FSDP options, etc.) are available unchanged – the wrapper simply forwards them to the underlying TRL trainer.

What makes **`RFSFTConfig`** different is that each argument can be supplied as:

* a single value (as in the original `SFTConfig`), **or**  
* a **`list`** of values, or a **`Range`** object, enabling RapidFire’s *multi‑config* specification (you can generate a grid of trainer configurations automatically).

RapidFire AI is an AI‑experiment execution framework that turns slow, sequential LLM‑pipeline customizations into fast, hyper‑parallel, dynamically‑controlled workflows with automatic backend optimization.  

It uniquely provides **live three‑way communication** among:

1. **Your IDE** – where you launch and script the experiment,  
2. **A metrics display/control dashboard** – showing real‑time results and letting you steer runs, and  
3. **The multi‑core/multi‑GPU execution backend** – which actually runs the training/evaluation shards.

The documentation lists three RAG/context‑engineering tutorials:

| Tutorial | Demonstrated workflow |
|----------|-----------------------|
| **FiQA RAG Q&A chatbot** | **All‑local model** – the entire pipeline runs on a locally hosted model. |
| **SciFact RAG for scientific claim verification** | **All‑OpenAI** – the pipeline uses OpenAI services for embedding, retrieval, and generation. |
| **GSM8K few‑shot / context‑engineering for math reasoning** | **Hybrid workflow** – combines local components (e.g., retrieval) with OpenAI calls (e.g., generation). |

The **`postprocess_fn`** is an optional, user‑supplied callable that receives a batch dictionary (which includes the model’s generated outputs under the reserved key **`"generated_text"`**) and returns a new or modified batch dictionary.  
Its purpose is to perform any per‑batch transformations needed before metrics are calculated—e.g., extracting structured fields from the generations, adding ground‑truth data, or otherwise reshaping the batch.

**When it runs:**  
During `run_evals`, the function is called **once for each batch, after the generation step has completed and **right before** the user‑provided `compute_metrics_fn` is invoked.  

So the order is:  

1. `preprocess_fn` → prepare inputs  
2. **Generation** → produce `generated_text`  
3. **`postprocess_fn`** → transform the batch (optional)  
4. `compute_metrics_fn` → compute metrics on the post‑processed batch.

RapidFire AI says that down‑sampling alone is a static, manual shortcut that misses the core benefits of its **online‑aggregation** engine:

* **You must pick a sample size up‑front** – a hard choice when eval metrics have high variance, and a wrong size can give misleading point estimates.  
* **No confidence intervals** – down‑sampled results are just point estimates, so you can get false confidence in a config.  
* **Manual re‑sampling is required** to reduce variance, which adds tedious file‑juggling and extra compute.  
* **No dynamic experiment control** – you cannot stop a poor config early, clone or modify a promising one on the fly, or resume/abort runs without re‑implementing that logic yourself.  
* **No automated parallelism or IC‑Ops** – down‑sampling does not leverage shard‑based parallel execution, token‑rate scheduling, or GPU/CPU allocation, so token spend and compute are often wasted on unproductive configs.

In contrast, RapidFire AI’s online aggregation shards the data, runs many configs in parallel, and streams **real‑time metric estimates with statistically‑sound confidence intervals**, letting you stop bad configs early, clone good ones, and continuously re‑allocate token/compute resources for maximum efficiency.

**Resolution steps**

1. **Identify stray Python processes**  
   ```bash
   ps -ef | grep python
   ```  
   Look for any processes labeled *“multiprocessing.spawn”* or marked *defunct*.

2. **Kill the offending processes**  
   ```bash
   kill -9 <PID>
   ```  
   (replace `<PID>` with the process IDs you found).

3. **Wait ~2 minutes** – this gives the system time to clean up any remaining threads.

4. **Restart the notebook/kernel** (or the Python session) before launching the next experiment.

Following these steps clears the leftover processes that cause the  

```
ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'
```  

error that appears when running experiments back‑to‑back.

**RFModelConfig** is the RapidFire AI wrapper for a model definition.  
According to the documentation it accepts the following arguments:

| Argument | Type | Description |

| **`model_name`** | `str` | Required. The identifier used with Hugging Face’s `AutoModel.from_pretrained()`. It can be a model hub name (e.g., `"Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct"`) or a local checkpoint path. |
| **`tokenizer`** | `str`, *optional* | The Hugging Face tokenizer identifier. Usually the same string as `model_name`, but can be different. |

These are the explicitly documented parameters for `RFModelConfig`. Other knobs may exist (and can be `List` or `Range` valued) as described in the Multi‑Config Specification, but they are not listed in the provided context.

In RapidFire AI’s online‑aggregation engine the metric’s **aggregation semantics** determine how the per‑shard results are combined:

| **Metric type** | **What it means** | **What you must provide** |
|-----------------|-------------------|---------------------------|
| **Distributive** | The metric can be computed on each shard (batch) and then combined with a simple, built‑in algebra (e.g., sum, count, average). No extra code is needed – if you don’t supply an `accumulate_metrics_fn`, all metrics returned by `compute_metrics_fn` are treated as distributive. | Nothing extra; the engine aggregates them automatically. |
| **Algebraic** | The metric’s final value cannot be obtained by a naïve sum/average of shard‑level values; it needs a custom reduction (e.g., variance, F1‑score, or any metric that requires both numerator and denominator to be merged in a specific way). | You must supply an `accumulate_metrics_fn` that knows how to combine the algebraic pieces across batches. |

So, **distributive metrics are directly aggregatable by the system, while algebraic metrics require a user‑provided aggregation function to correctly combine the intermediate results.**
